payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.

parsed.text:
The graph already captures the sole requested edit and appropriately distinguishes a completed pencil drawing from partial progress, no progress, and uncertainty. The evaluation’s valid judgments consistently call this edit partial: the image is desaturated and grainy, but still reads largely as a filtered photograph rather than a pencil drawing. Preserve that distinction; do not loosen the completion criterion to reward color reduction or texture alone.

The main weakness is that the current partial criterion may be too narrow: it requires visible pencil-drawing linework and tonal rendering, so an image with clear pencil-like shading or contours but less obvious linework could be under-credited. Refine the criterion to assess the overall visual medium—whether the image convincingly reads as a pencil drawing through characteristic drawn contours, graphite-like tonal marks, and texture—without requiring every feature in every region. Keep partial for a recognizable but incomplete or uneven conversion, and absent for no discernible pencil-style transformation. This should improve consistency while avoiding answer-coded thresholds.

The supplied edited image supports partial rather than complete: it retains the source composition and substantial photographic detail, while muted color and grain provide some stylization but not a convincing pencil-drawn rendering. No additional requirement or support check is needed; retain one requested check for the single instruction, and keep uncertainty reserved for genuinely unassessable images rather than treating ambiguous style as absence.
